examples.source: BBC News, “Warnings about junk mail deluge”

examples.text: The second answer is, that the existence of such a power in the Constitution will have a strong influence in giving efficacy to requisitions.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: Insolent or impertinent behavior; shameless boldness.
etymology: From French effronterie, from Late Latin effrons "shameless," from ex- "out" + frons "forehead." Barefaced, putting one's forehead forward.

examples.text: He was not in truth much surprised at Mr. Slope's effrontery, but he was obliged to act as though he had been to save his daughter's feelings.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: He stood close to her, and the effrontery in his eyes repelled the old, vanishing self in her, yet drew all her awakening sensuousness.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

examples.text: I wonder—yes I wonder how he has the effrontery to look me in the face, to dare to claim acquaintance with me.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: Fluent or persuasive in speaking or writing; clearly expressive.
etymology: From Latin eloqui "to speak out," from e- "out" + loqui "to speak" (compare "loquacious").

examples.text: What can I add to Mr. Forsyth's eloquently put arguments... except applause!
Pan Mussyalovitch had indeed sent an extremely long and characteristically eloquent letter in which he begged her to lend him three roubles.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: Their newly found economic strength is eloquent testimony to the striking success of the policies of economic cooperation which we and they have pursued.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: To match or surpass a person or achievement, typically by imitation.
etymology: From Latin aemulari "to rival," from aemulus "rivaling."

examples.text: The game has also tried to emulate franchises such as Jak and Daxter and Ratchet and Clank on PS2 and so there are a number of combat elements.
"It's ironic," says Walsh, "that we are looking at the possibility of emulating something that has now been replaced by something much closer to what we've currently got."
I will endeavour, in my relations with Mrs. Merridew, to emulate the moderation which Betteredge displays in his relations with me.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

definition: To cause someone to feel drained of energy or vitality; to weaken. (It does not mean "energize.")
etymology: From Latin enervare "to weaken," literally "to remove the sinews," from e- "out" + nervus "sinew."

examples.text: Enervated, prostrate, and breathless, he became unconscious of outward objects; he seemed to be entering that vague delirium preceding death.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: If he possesses an unusual share of native energy, or the enervating magic of place do not operate too long upon him, his forfeited powers may be redeemable.
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

examples.text: An artful cabal in that council would be able to distract and to enervate the whole system of administration.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: A person or thing that is mysterious, puzzling, or difficult to understand.
etymology: From Greek ainigma "riddle," from ainissesthai "to speak in riddles."

examples.text: One of them came from the enigmatic Robben when he jinked his way through two Arsenal defenders only to see his poked shot saved by Almunia.
Scientists say they've solved a decade-old puzzle about the enigmatic 'strange quark', one of the fundamental building blocks of matter.
Daniel felt the presence of a new guest who seemed to come with an enigmatic veiled face, and to carry dimly-conjectured, dreaded revelations.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Lasting for a very short time.
etymology: From Greek ephēmeros "lasting only a day," from epi- "on" + hēmera "day."

examples.text: Georges says unlike other turtles, Chelodina longicollis has evolved the ability to take long overland hikes because it prefers ephemeral waters, such as temporary swamps and pools.
In fact, if there could be any hope, it would be very ephemeral, because there would be no claim for assistance in that case, far from it....
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: They talked on slight and ephemeral subjects, and when his tea was brought up he told the amazed little servant that a cup was to be set for Sue.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: Mental calmness and composure, especially in a difficult situation.
etymology: From Latin aequanimitas, from aequus "even" + animus "mind."

examples.text: And therefore he will be least likely to lament, and will bear with the greatest equanimity any misfortune of this sort which may befall him.
examples.author: Plato (tr. Benjamin Jowett)

examples.text: An exhausted composure, a worn-out placidity, an equanimity of fatigue not to be ruffled by interest or satisfaction, are the trophies of her victory.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: But suddenly something happened which was very annoying and unpleasant for every one in the house, and completely upset Fyodor Pavlovitch's equanimity at once.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: To use ambiguous language so as to conceal the truth or avoid committing oneself.
etymology: From Late Latin aequivocare "to call by the same name," from aequus "equal" + vocare "to call."

examples.text: He made a curious grimace—one of his strange and equivocal demonstrations—threw down his cue and followed me from the room.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: Jos had always had rather a mean opinion of the Captain, and now began to think his courage was somewhat equivocal.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: The three who had risen fell away from Gogol, and that equivocal person himself resumed his seat.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

definition: Having or showing great knowledge or learning.
etymology: From Latin eruditus "instructed," from erudire "to polish," literally "to bring out of roughness," from e- "out" + rudis "rough, untrained" (compare "rude").

examples.text: He had never been fond of Mr. Casaubon, and if it had not been for the sense of obligation, would have laughed at him as a Bat of erudition.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: In fact, his disappointment at the nature of those tongues had, after a while, been the means of still further glorifying the erudition of Christminster.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: But I delivered this written communication (slate and all) with my own hand, and Joe received it as a miracle of erudition.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Intended for or likely to be understood by only a small number of people with specialized knowledge.
etymology: From Greek esōterikos "belonging to an inner circle," from esōterō "further in." First applied to Pythagorean teaching meant for initiates.

examples.text: The merchants valued him not less than we, his esoteric friends.
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

examples.text: Two marquees had been erected for these two banquets: that for the quality on the esoteric or garden side of a certain deep ha-ha; and that for the non-quality on the exoteric or paddock side of the same.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: The life esoteric is not for ordinary person.
examples.author: James Joyce

definition: To make a problem, bad situation, or negative feeling worse.
etymology: From Latin exacerbare "to irritate," from ex- "thoroughly" + acerbus "harsh, bitter."

examples.text: Worries about the size of insurance liabilities dragged European shares down, although the impact was exacerbated by light post-Christmas trading.
examples.source: BBC News, “Asian quake hits European shares”

examples.text: Iran had warned the United States earlier in the day against exacerbating the Gulf crisis, saying military action would endanger American interests.
examples.source: Reuters, “Diplomats Call U.S. Attack On Oil Rig Restrained”

examples.text: The licensing changes have sparked concern among some MPs, councils and some senior police officers who fear they could exacerbate drinking problems.
examples.source: BBC News, “Police urge pub closure power”

definition: To show or declare that someone is not guilty of wrongdoing.
etymology: From Medieval Latin exculpare, from ex- "out of" + culpa "blame."

examples.text: She was helped home by poor Susan and treacherous Mrs. Betty, who, now the mischief was done, thought only of exculpating herself to her master.
examples.author: Maria Edgeworth

examples.text: Two months passed away in hopeless expectation on my part, while I must do the magistrate the justice to say that he used every means to obtain information of the person I declared could exculpate me if he would.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: The bishop thought it necessary to exculpate himself.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: To praise enthusiastically.
etymology: From Latin extollere "to raise up," from ex- "out, up" + tollere "to raise."

examples.text: I extolled her beauty, her gaiety, her wit, so warmly, that my praises excited in him a desire to see a damsel adorned by such attractions.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: As he had continued to look steadily at me, I took it as a reminder that he objected to being extolled for his consideration.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: It is the humor of many heads to extol the days of their forefathers, and declaim against the wickedness of times present.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Very attentive to accuracy and detail; very concerned about matters of cleanliness or taste.
etymology: From Latin fastidiosus "disdainful, squeamish," from fastidium "loathing."

examples.text: The count appeared, dressed with the greatest simplicity, but the most fastidious dandy could have found nothing to cavil at in his toilet.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: Aye, I said, I knew all along that a fastidious gentleman like you would not be contented with the thoughts of other people about these matters.
examples.author: Plato (tr. Benjamin Jowett)

examples.text: She fluttered toward the tailor shop, dashed into its slovenly heat with the comic fastidiousness of a humming bird dipping into a dry tiger-lily.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: Having or displaying a passionate intensity.
etymology: From Latin fervere "to boil, glow."

examples.text: But the release of the first full version of Firefox has managed to drum up a respectable amount of pre-launch fervour.
examples.source: BBC News, “Firefox browser takes on Microsoft”

examples.text: How lovingly and fervently did it commend the pretty creature I had won, with all her artless graces best displayed, to my most gentle care!
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: And tonight I call on all our allies and peace-loving nations throughout the world to join us with renewed fervor in a global effort to combat terrorism.
examples.author: Bill Clinton

definition: Excessively talkative, especially on trivial matters.
etymology: From Latin garrulus, from garrire "to chatter."

examples.text: Disdaining the heroic outfit, excitable in her methods, garrulous, episodical, shrill, she misled her lover much as she had misled her aunt.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: Now and then came a flash of cockney humour, now and then some old lady, a character such as Charles Dickens might have drawn, would amuse them by her garrulous oddities.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: In this state of second childhood, it had an air of being in its own way garrulous about its early life.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Fond of company; sociable. (Of animals) living in flocks or herds.
etymology: From Latin gregarius, from grex "flock, herd" (also in "congregate" and "egregious").

examples.text: The normally gregarious Evans cut a peculiarly unshowbusiness-like figure as he sipped coffee and smoked cigarettes, wrapped in a big coat and scarf in front of his Aladdin's cave.
examples.source: BBC News, “Chris Evans back on the market”

examples.text: Even now I am certain that those seas are not, and perhaps never can be, in the present constitution of things, a place for his habitual gregarious resort.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: The contrary instincts and inclinations now attain to moral honour, the gregarious instinct gradually draws its conclusions.
examples.author: Friedrich Nietzsche (tr. Helen Zimmern)

definition: Sly or cunning intelligence.
etymology: From Old French guile "deceit," probably of Germanic origin, related to "wile."

examples.text: This guileless confectioner was not by any means sober, and had a black eye in the green stage of recovery, which was painted over.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: She looked on with some amusement.—Miss Bates's gratitude for Mrs. Elton's attentions to Jane was in the first style of guileless simplicity and warmth.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: She knew that he loved her—a frank, blustering fellow without guile enough to conceal his feelings, and no desire to do so.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

definition: A lengthy and aggressive speech; to lecture someone at length in an aggressive manner.
etymology: From Old French arenge, from Medieval Latin harenga, probably from a Germanic word for an assembly or a crowd.

examples.text: The International Rugby Board may have to step in to stop frustrated coaches and players from publicly haranguing referees when things go belly-up.
When Lebeziatnikov finished his long-winded harangue with the logical deduction at the end, he was quite tired, and the perspiration streamed from his face.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: But the venom of the chaplain's harangue had worked into his blood, and sapped the life of his sweet contentment.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: Acting or done quickly and without thought or care.
etymology: From Latin impetus "attack, force," from impetere "to rush upon."

examples.text: She turned away and was about to ask the countess again how to go to him, when light, impetuous, and seemingly buoyant steps were heard at the door.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: With those words uttered impetuously, Will rose, put out his hand to Rosamond, still with the air of a somnambulist, and went away.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Then impetuously he told her that Mildred had left him and that his unhappiness had been so great that he almost killed himself.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: Unable to be appeased or placated; relentless.
etymology: From Latin implacabilis, from in- "not" + placare "to appease" (compare "placate").

examples.text: Her iron-grey hair hung in heavy bands on either side of her face—her dark eyes looked straight forward, with a hard, defiant, implacable stare.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: With these words, and a laugh, and laying a bitter stress on the word "ladyship," Mrs. Chadband folds her arms and looks implacably at Mr. Bucket.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Not a word more would he say, but sat in his implacable sullenness as indifferent to me as though I had not been in the room at all.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

definition: Not in harmony or keeping with the surroundings or other aspects of something.
etymology: From Latin incongruus, from in- "not" + congruus "agreeing."

examples.text: "It's within the same concept but it's incongruous, it's the mismatch... it's not the fact that you've fallen onto your backside."
Obstacles, incongruities, all melted into the sense of completion with which his soul was flooded by this outward satisfaction of his longing.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: The negative upon the acts of the legislative by the executive authority, and that in the hands of one individual, would seem to be an incongruity in our system.
examples.author: William Henry Harrison

definition: Wanting to avoid activity or exertion; lazy.
etymology: From Late Latin indolens "not feeling pain," from in- "not" + dolere "to suffer." Painless became "taking no trouble."

examples.text: Eliza generally took no more notice of her sister's indolence and complaints than if no such murmuring, lounging object had been before her.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: He was one of those, who, liking work, knew how to do it, and despite his indolence would sometimes spend a whole night at his writing table.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: When the first transports of rage which had produced his activity in seeking her were over, he naturally returned to all his former indolence.
examples.author: Jane Austen

definition: Too great or extreme to be expressed or described in words.
etymology: From Latin ineffabilis, from in- "not" + effabilis "utterable," from effari "to speak out."

examples.text: It is an ineffably oozy, stringy affair, most frequently found in the tubs of sperm, after a prolonged squeezing, and subsequent decanting.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: "You don't expect anybody to believe this, about the lady and the sovereign, do you?" says the constable, eyeing him aside with ineffable disdain.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: This was not the discomposure of last night; that had quite passed—such discomposures were a detail; the real coercion was to see a man ineffably adored.
examples.author: Henry James

definition: Impossible to stop or prevent; (of a person) impossible to persuade.
etymology: From Latin inexorabilis, from in- "not" + exorare "to prevail upon by entreaty," from orare "to pray."

examples.text: However, in the face of sterling's apparently inexorable climb, the authorities today decided to cede to pressure and allow a half-point cut.
examples.source: Reuters, “U.K. Issues One Billion Stg Bond Tranche”

examples.text: The proliferation of gadgets in our homes is inexorably altering the role of the high street in our lives thinks Mr Vaughan.
examples.source: BBC News, “Sony PSP tipped as a 'must-have'”

examples.text: If he was by an inexorable logic to pay for it he was literally impatient to know the cost, and he held himself ready to pay in instalments.
examples.author: Henry James

definition: Innocent, unsuspecting, and candid. (Do not confuse with ingenious, "clever.")
etymology: From Latin ingenuus "native, freeborn," hence "noble, frank."

examples.text: It would be a unique delight to wait and watch for the melodious fragments in which her heart and soul came forth so directly and ingenuously.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: He rose with a start, his ingenuous face looking as though it had been dipped in crimson: even the reddish tint in his beard seemed to deepen.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: Nor did his blushes and awkwardness take away from it: she was pleased with these healthy tokens of the young gentleman's ingenuousness.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: Lacking flavor; lacking vigor or interest.
etymology: From Late Latin insipidus, from in- "not" + sapidus "tasty," from sapere "to taste, be wise" (also in "sapient").

examples.text: The eaters of the dinner, like the dinner itself, were lukewarm, insipid, overdone—and all owing to this poor little dull Young Barnacle.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: The waves were colourless, and the Bournemouth steamer gave a further touch of insipidity, drawn up against the pier and hooting wildly for excursionists.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: The news that "Bony" was come back from Egypt was comparatively insipid, and the repulse of the French in Italy was nothing to Mrs. Poyser's repulse of the old squire.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Unwilling or refusing to change one's views or to agree about something.
etymology: From Spanish los intransigentes, the name of an extreme republican party in the 1870s, from Latin in- "not" + transigere "to come to an agreement."

examples.text: Employers organization chairman, Jacques Schoufour, accused the FNV of intransigence in refusing to alter its stance at all over the past two months.
examples.source: Reuters, “Neither Side Optimistic On Rotterdam Port Issues”

examples.text: Jorge Cardenas, manager of the national federation and head of his nation's delegation in London, has blamed the intransigence of some big countries, without naming them.
examples.source: Reuters, “Colombia Coffee Exporters Believe In Pragmatism”

examples.text: Tesfay accused the West of intransigence in the negotiation of recent commodity agreements.
examples.source: Reuters, “Ethiopia Minister Sees Africa Debt Payment Problem”

definition: Fearless; adventurous.
etymology: From Latin intrepidus, from in- "not" + trepidus "alarmed" (compare "trepidation").

examples.text: Not only do mythical figures like the Amazons, the god Apollo or the sirens of Homeric lore appear in space, but Star Trek contains the sweeping themes of intrepid adventure and bold exploration that lie at the heart of classical mythology.
She had thought that of course Tom had deserted long ago, and she wondered at seeing him place himself in her power again in this intrepid way.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: It spoke in a voice harsh and lugubrious but intrepid, and little by little it dawned upon Archie that this was a development of the Patna case.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

definition: To flood; to overwhelm someone with things to be dealt with.
etymology: From Latin inundare, from in- "onto" + unda "a wave."

examples.text: The barring of non-US visitors has led to the campaign being inundated with calls and forced it to make a statement about why the blocking was taking place.
examples.source: BBC News, “Attack prompts Bush site block”

examples.text: "We have the beer, but distribution and sales is the important point," van Schaik said, adding that since the ruling Heineken had been inundated by German traders seeking joint ventures.
examples.source: Reuters, “Heineken Sees Higher Profits, Wider Penetration”

examples.text: Here and there, especially at first, the inundation started on them and swept by; but when they had done descending, and were winding and climbing up a tower, they were alone.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Using very few words.
etymology: From Greek Lakōnikos "of Laconia," the region around Sparta. Spartans were famed for curt speech; when Philip II of Macedon threatened "If I invade Laconia...," they reportedly replied, "If."

examples.text: Jude did not pause to remember that, in the laconic words of the historian, "insulted Nature sometimes vindicated her rights" in such circumstances.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: But their father, though very laconic in his expressions of pleasure, was really glad to see them; he had felt their importance in the family circle.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: Mr Plornish, as being of a more laconic temperament, embraced this opportunity of interposing with the suggestion that she should now leave Mr Clennam to himself.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Displaying or having a disinclination for physical exertion; relaxed and slow; weak or faint.
etymology: From Latin languidus "faint, weak," from languere "to be weak."

examples.text: It was not a scorching, hard, dusty day like the treacherous intruder of a week before, but soaked with languor, softened with a milky light.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: The wind shook some blossoms from the trees, and the heavy lilac-blooms, with their clustering stars, moved to and fro in the languid air.
examples.author: Oscar Wilde

examples.text: Yet, in spite of all this, Anne had reason to believe that she had moments only of languor and depression, to hours of occupation and enjoyment.
examples.author: Jane Austen

definition: Affected by a lack of energy or enthusiasm; sluggish.
etymology: From Greek lēthargos "forgetful," from lēthē "forgetfulness." Lethe was the river of forgetting in the underworld.

examples.text: Indeed, it was the visitors who looked likelier to enliven a drab opening played at a lethargic pace.
examples.source: BBC News, “Chelsea denied by James heroics”

examples.text: The French primary bond market is showing signs of renewed effervescence after several weeks of lethargy and the trend is expected to continue if hopes of imminent interest rate cuts are fulfilled, market operators said.
examples.source: Reuters, “French Primary Bond Market Shows New Sparkle”

examples.text: The gaunt rooms, deserted for years upon years, seemed to have settled down into a gloomy lethargy from which nothing could rouse them again.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Tending to talk a great deal; talkative.
etymology: From Latin loquax "talkative," from loqui "to speak."

examples.text: Pedestrians are also out in force, and are a loquacious bunch.
examples.source: BBC News, “GTA sequel is criminally good”

examples.text: They began to talk, and finding Clutton more loquacious and less sardonic than usual, Philip determined to take advantage of his good humour.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: Uncle Glegg stood open-mouthed with astonishment at this unembarrassed loquacity, with which his understanding could hardly keep pace.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Expressed clearly and easy to understand; showing an ability to think clearly.
etymology: From Latin lucidus "bright," from lux "light."

examples.text: The game's visual quality would be "like a lucid dream," said Mr Cameron.
examples.source: BBC News, “New consoles promise big problems”

examples.text: But he rode home with a terribly lucid vision of the difficulty there would be in arranging any result that could be permanently counted on with this man.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Mr Plornish amiably growled, in his philosophical but not lucid manner, that there was ups you see, and there was downs.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Very generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone less powerful.
etymology: From Latin magnanimus, from magnus "great" + animus "soul."

examples.text: I regard you in any case as a man of noble character and not without elements of magnanimity, though I don't agree with all your convictions.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: In spite of this magnanimity Dorothea was still smarting: perhaps as much from Celia's subdued astonishment as from her small criticisms.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: They have claims on the magnanimity and, I may add, on the justice of this nation which we must all feel.
examples.author: James Monroe

definition: A person who dislikes humankind and avoids human society.
etymology: From Greek misanthrōpos, from misein "to hate" + anthrōpos "human being." Popularized by Molière's play Le Misanthrope (1666).

examples.text: Like a plethoric burning martyr, or a self-consuming misanthrope, once ignited, the whale supplies his own fuel and burns by his own body.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: A perfect misanthropist's heaven: and Mr. Heathcliff and I are such a suitable pair to divide the desolation between us.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

examples.text: All the world used her ill, said this young misanthropist, and we may be pretty certain that persons whom all the world treats ill, deserve entirely the treatment they get.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: To make something bad less severe, serious, or painful.
etymology: From Latin mitigare, from mitis "mild, soft" + agere "to make."

examples.text: In most of these cases, the scientists speculate that the leaf mash might have been used to mitigate topical skin infections or repel bugs.
"We are looking to mitigate an exposure, cost to growers, by potentially diverting some of those vessels to other markets," he said.
Here also the firmness of the judicial magistracy is of vast importance in mitigating the severity and confining the operation of such laws.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: To appease the anger or anxiety of someone.
etymology: From Latin mollificare "to soften," from mollis "soft."

examples.text: But some analysts said Japan's attempt to mollify the U.S. was a double edged sword, and might be read at a subtle form of trade retaliation for the tariffs proposed by the U.S.
examples.source: Reuters, “Japan Cuts Chip Supply, May Produce Shortage”

examples.text: Analytical Chemist goes to the door, confers angrily with unseen tapper, appears to become mollified by descrying reason in the tapping, and goes out.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: "Dear, dear friend!" she said, with a touch of such natural feeling, that Miss Briggs of course at once began to melt, and even the bathing-woman was mollified.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: Sullen and ill-tempered.
etymology: From Latin morosus "peevish, fastidious," from mos "custom, manner." Being set in one's ways became being sour about it.

examples.text: Ferguson appeared to be a morose and silent man, but I could see from the little that he said that he was at least a fellow-countryman.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

examples.text: The count ordered his carriage that he might drive to Sokolniki, and sat in his study with folded hands, morose, sallow, and taciturn.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: Dorset, of late, had grown more than usually morose and incalculable, and Ned Silverton went about with an air that seemed to challenge the universe.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course of action.
etymology: From Latin obdurare "to harden," from ob- "against" + durus "hard."

examples.text: This old man wears a hat, a thumbed and napless and yet an obdurate hat, which has never adapted itself to the shape of his poor head.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: May I die if the enchanters that persecute me are not trying to entangle me in them and delay my journey, by way of revenge for my obduracy towards Altisidora.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: She came, but refused to kiss them: it was such hard luck on the little things, she said, and though Dolly proffered Chorly-worly and Porgly-woggles in turn, she was obdurate.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: Obedient or attentive to an excessive or servile degree.
etymology: From Latin obsequiosus "compliant," from obsequi "to comply," from ob- "toward" + sequi "to follow."

examples.text: Philip flushed, all the more because the surgeon spoke obviously with a humorous intention, and his brow-beaten dressers laughed obsequiously.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: The cavalcade passed out by the lower gate of Phoenix park saluted by obsequious policemen and proceeded past Kingsbridge along the northern quays.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: Whenever Mr. Snagsby and his conductors are stationary, the crowd flows round, and from its squalid depths obsequious advice heaves up to Mr. Bucket.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or chosen course of action, despite attempts to persuade.
etymology: From Latin obstinatus "determined," from obstinare "to persist."

examples.text: The money market head said the unions' humiliation by the protracted financial problems of the Neue Heimat cooperative housing venture would contribute to union obstinacy.
examples.source: Reuters, “German Wage Round Said To Limit Monetary Options”

examples.text: With regard to a large number of matters about which other men are decided or obstinate, he was the most easily manageable man in the world.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: He always took her hand as though with repugnance, always seemed vexed to meet her and was sometimes obstinately silent throughout her visit.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: To remove a need or difficulty; to avoid or prevent.
etymology: From Late Latin obviare "to meet in the way, prevent," from ob viam "in the way."

examples.text: "These technological advances could potentially obviate the need for geological repositories altogether."
The propositions which have been made for supplying the omission have rather served to illustrate than to obviate the difficulty of the thing.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: In order to obviate any delays possible through any routine requirements as to payment in your departments, we enclose cheque herewith for ten pounds (L10), receipt of which please acknowledge.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

definition: Assertive of authority in an annoyingly domineering way, especially about trivial matters; meddlesome.
etymology: From Latin officiosus "obliging, dutiful," from officium "service, duty." Being eager to serve tipped into meddling.

examples.text: Margaret Schlegel has been officious and tiresome during this terrible week, and we have all suffered under her, but upon my soul she's honest.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: You don't know how the cursed carelessness that is over-officious in helping me at every other turning of my life, WON'T help me here.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: How this charmingly convenient obstacle could have escaped the officious penetration of the Count, it was impossible to conceive—but it HAD escaped him.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

definition: Involving a great deal of effort, trouble, or difficulty; burdensome.
etymology: From Latin onerosus, from onus "a load, burden."

examples.text: The SEC said it had taken into consideration the fact that foreign companies were already working to meet more onerous financial reporting rules in their home countries.
examples.source: BBC News, “US gives foreign firms extra time”

examples.text: But Federal Industry Minister, Ian Macfarlane, says a mandatory code would have been too onerous.
I think on the whole the bishop was right, for though the services required will not be of a very onerous nature, they will be more so than they were before.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: Characterized by vulgar or pretentious display, designed to impress.
etymology: From Latin ostentare "to display," frequentative of ostendere "to show."

examples.text: However, the ostentation of some of the items on sale painted a picture of the eccentricity that endeared him to the British public in shows such as Channel 4's gameshow Don't Forget Your Toothbrush.
examples.source: BBC News, “Chris Evans back on the market”

examples.text: He carried his fat paunch with ostentation on his short legs, and during the time his gang infested the station spoke to no one but his nephew.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: Our honesty, we free spirits—let us be careful lest it become our vanity, our ornament and ostentation, our limitation, our stupidity!
examples.author: Friedrich Nietzsche (tr. Helen Zimmern)

definition: A person or thing regarded as a perfect example of a particular quality.
etymology: From Italian paragone "touchstone," a stone used to test the purity of gold, from Greek parakonan "to sharpen against."

examples.text: Down in Bleeding Heart Yard, where there was not one unappropriated halfpenny, as lively an interest was taken in this paragon of men as on the Stock Exchange.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: From heaven the hero must be smiling down upon that paragon of a boy whom he had left to comfort and console her.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: The suggestion, it is true, was a faint one, but then Dardanelov was such a paragon of purity and delicacy that it was enough for the time being to make him perfectly happy.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: The presence of something in only small or insufficient quantities.
etymology: From Latin paucitas, from paucus "few" (related to "paltry" and "poor").

examples.text: "With the paucity of contrary evidence, the hills are presumed to be anthropogenic structures of potentially colossal proportions," says Bosnian geophysicist Dr Amer Smailbegovic.

Nashashibi said lack of experience among Arab banks, a paucity of financial instruments and a legal framework that often does not recognise the western banking concept of interest have hampered the growth of Arab markets.
examples.source: Reuters, “Arab Banker Says Too Soon For Single Currency”

examples.text: Any inward debate Lydgate had as to the consequences of this engagement which had stolen upon him, turned on the paucity of time rather than of money.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Excessively concerned with minor details or rules; overscrupulous.
etymology: From Italian pedante "teacher, schoolmaster," perhaps from Greek paideuein "to teach."

examples.text: His gentleness was never tinged by dogmatism, and his instructions were given with an air of frankness and good nature that banished every idea of pedantry.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: Perhaps it need not be done so pedantically, thought Nicholas, or even done at all, but this untiring, continual spiritual effort of which the sole aim was the children's moral welfare delighted him.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: "He's a cursed white-blooded pedantic coxcomb," said Will, with gnashing impetuosity.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Carried out with a minimum of effort or reflection, merely as a routine duty.
etymology: From Late Latin perfunctorius "careless," from perfungi "to get through with, discharge."

examples.text: Now and again he would emit a bothered perfunctory "Sssh," which neither produced nor was expected to produce the slightest effect.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: She had invented a way of meeting them—as if he had been a polite perfunctory poor relation, of distant degree—that made them almost ridiculous in him.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: Reforms in the civil service must go on; but the changes should be real and genuine, not perfunctory, or prompted by a zeal in behalf of any party simply because it happens to be in power.
examples.author: William McKinley

definition: Having a harmful effect, especially in a gradual or subtle way.
etymology: From Latin perniciosus "destructive," from pernicies "ruin," from per- "completely" + nex "death."

examples.text: The pernicious program opens a backdoor on a computer so it can be controlled remotely by malicious hackers.
examples.source: BBC News, “Beckham virus spotted on the net”

examples.text: Despite that pernicious assumption of lassitude and indifference, which had become his second nature, he was strongly attached to his friend.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: It will furnish absolute security which makes the proposed scheme of government guaranty of deposits so alluring, without its pernicious results.
examples.author: William Howard Taft

definition: To make someone less angry or hostile.
etymology: From Latin placare "to soothe," related to placere "to please."

examples.text: They say Mr Ellison may be trying to placate Peoplesoft customers riled by Oracle's determined takeover strategy.
examples.source: BBC News, “Jobs go at Oracle after takeover”

examples.text: But today's smaller than expected rate cut appeared to have placated markets for now, analysts said.
examples.source: Reuters, “U.K. Base Rates Will Fall Again Soon, Say Analysts”

examples.text: His manner of sneering at what he called "parlor socialists" (though the phrase was not overwhelmingly new) had a power which made her wish to placate his company of well-fed, speed-loving administrators.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: Dealing with things sensibly and realistically, based on practical rather than theoretical considerations.
etymology: From Greek pragmatikos "relating to affairs," from pragma "deed, thing done."

examples.text: Using Braille for speeches, and briefed by his officials on tape, he also has a sharp tongue at times, and a pragmatic approach to politics.
Arango said that government measures adopted here last week, including a lower export registration price, indicated a major change but also disclosed a welcome pragmatism.
examples.source: Reuters, “Colombia Coffee Exporters Believe In Pragmatism”

examples.text: They represent a pragmatic rededication to social compassion and national excellence, in place of the combination of good intentions and fuzzy follow-through which too often in the past was thought sufficient.
examples.author: Richard Nixon

definition: To speak or act in an evasive way; to avoid telling the whole truth.
etymology: From Latin praevaricari "to walk crookedly," from prae- "before" + varicare "to straddle," from varus "bent, knock-kneed."

examples.text: The bubble of frustration against what appears as Japanese prevarication burst last week.
examples.source: Reuters, “Japan Isolated, Yen Rises, World Feels Cheated”

examples.text: Barbara denied, prevaricated, stammered, and at last was overcome with confusion; for which even the most indulgent spectators could scarcely pity her.
examples.author: Maria Edgeworth

examples.text: It was nevertheless no light matter that the very effect of his confusion should be to make him again prevaricate.
examples.author: Henry James

definition: In its original condition; unspoiled; clean and fresh as if new.
etymology: From Latin pristinus "former, early." The sense "spotless, new" developed only in the 20th century.

examples.text: The draft policy aims to protect 19 of the state's pristine river catchments, by introducing restrictions on agriculture, aquaculture and grazing.
A seven-year quest to return to Earth pristine samples from the solar system's formation ended in triumph in a dark and wet Utah desert at the weekend.
And the separation is essential to the preservation of that institution in its pristine purity.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: Spending money or resources freely and recklessly; wastefully extravagant. As a noun, a person who leaves and returns repentant.
etymology: From Latin prodigus "wasteful," from prodigere "to drive away, squander." The Prodigal Son parable (Luke 15) gave the noun sense.

examples.text: At this festival the magnificence displayed was such as had not been known in the little German place since the days of the prodigal Victor XIV.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: Permit me to give an idea of my devotion to my aunt's interests by recording that, on this occasion, I committed the prodigality of taking a cab.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: The toleration of this idea results in the waste of the people's money by their chosen servants and encourages prodigality and extravagance in the home life of our countrymen.
examples.author: Grover Cleveland

definition: Recklessly extravagant or wasteful; licentious, dissolute.
etymology: From Latin profligatus "ruined, dissolute," from profligare "to strike down."

examples.text: Then followed a paragraph giving other examples of such heroes and Saviours being born of some profligate intercourse between God and mortal.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: These were the very words of the old profligate, who felt already that his death was not far off and who actually died five months later.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: We should not permit our great prosperity to lead us to reckless ventures in business or profligacy in public expenditures.
examples.author: William McKinley

definition: An inclination or natural tendency to behave in a particular way.
etymology: From Latin propensus "inclined," from propendere "to hang forward."

examples.text: In general, these squid tend to be solitary, unromantic animals with a propensity to cannibalise their neighbours and take sexual favours by force, he says.

The paper's reasoning is complex, and is based on a sophisticated model of the relationship between tax regimes and corporate governance - in particular, the propensity of management to steal from the company.
examples.source: BBC News, “Could Yukos be a blessing in disguise?”

examples.text: And Herbert had seen him as a predatory Tartar of comic propensities, with a face like a red brick, and an outrageous hat all over bells.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Having the style or diction of prose; lacking poetic beauty; commonplace and dull.
etymology: From Late Latin prosaicus, from prosa "prose," from prosa oratio "straightforward speech."

examples.text: There was in Lily a vein of sentiment, perhaps transmitted from this source, which gave an idealizing touch to her most prosaic purposes.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: It was hard to believe that amongst so prosaic surroundings of neglect and dust and decay there was any ground for such fear as already we knew.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: Others, however, may rather maintain that this very iteration is an original felicity, to which none but the most prosaic minds can be insensible.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Acting with or showing care and thought for the future.
etymology: Contracted from Latin providens "foreseeing," from providere "to see ahead" (the root of "provide").

examples.text: "I may add that we are perilously close to the limits of fiscal prudence and there is no more room for spending beyond our means," he said.
"There is no assurance the bank will receive acceptable offers or be sold, but we feel this is a prudent step to take at this time," the bank said.
The Florentines appointed as their captain Pagolo Vitelli, a most prudent man, who from a private position had risen to the greatest renown.
examples.author: Niccolò Machiavelli (tr. W. K. Marriott)

definition: Complaining in a petulant or whining manner.
etymology: From Latin querulus, from queri "to complain" (also the source of "quarrel").

examples.text: Thereafter Cornelius did not open his lips except to ask querulously for somebody to bale out his canoe, which was towing behind the long-boat.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: He was interested in the human side of that struggle to express something which was so obscure in the man's mind that he was become morbid and querulous.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: Lisbeth was going on, for she was not at all afraid of Seth, and usually poured into his ears all the querulousness which was repressed by her awe of Adam.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: In a state or period of inactivity or dormancy.
etymology: From Latin quiescere "to become quiet," from quies "rest."

examples.text: In a second study published in the same journal, UK researchers say they found one important protein that keeps stem cells in a quiescent and non-dividing stage.
He never omitted the ceremony afterwards, and the gravity and quiescence with which I underwent it, seemed to invest it for him with a certain charm.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: If Edgar Linton meets me, I shall not hesitate to knock him down, and give him enough to insure his quiescence while I stay.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

definition: Bitterness or resentfulness, especially when long-standing.
etymology: From Late Latin rancor "rankness, rancid smell," from rancere "to stink" (compare "rancid").

examples.text: It began with a flood of publicity which helped UKIP into third place in last June's European elections but became dominated by rancour as he tried to take over the party leadership.

The U.S. Expects more harmonious talks than usual during French Prime Minister Jacques Chirac's first official visit this week as frequently rancorous disputes between the two countries begin to fade.
examples.source: Reuters, “U.S. Sees More Harmony In Talks With France”

examples.text: He recognises the laws of the state and he can break them without sense of sin, but if he is punished he accepts the punishment without rancour.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: Having an obstinately uncooperative attitude toward authority or discipline.
etymology: From Latin recalcitrare "to kick back," from re- "back" + calx "heel," as a horse kicks.

examples.text: He had often thought of Arabella's remarks that he should have been more severe with Sue, that her recalcitrant spirit would soon have been broken.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: Behind her, waiting their turn to name themselves to the Countess, Archer noticed a number of the recalcitrant couples who had declined to meet her at Mrs. Lovell Mingott's.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: They shrank from the master who still strove for their chains; they fled to the friends that had freed them, even though those friends stood ready to use them as a club for driving the recalcitrant South back into loyalty.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

definition: To refuse to accept or be associated with; to deny the truth or validity of.
etymology: From Latin repudiare "to divorce, reject," from repudium "divorce."

examples.text: Poor Little Dorrit, not seeing her way to the offering of any soothing words that would escape repudiation, deemed it best to remain quiet.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: He could not disavow his actions, belauded as they were by half the world, and so he had to repudiate truth, goodness, and all humanity.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: He would pay for Mrs. Munt's hearth-rug with ostentatious haste, a large claim he would repudiate quietly, and fight court by court.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: Not revealing one's thoughts or feelings readily; reserved.
etymology: From Latin reticere "to keep silent," from re- (intensive) + tacere "to be silent" (compare "tacit").

examples.text: "Although his films vary in style, they all bear his unmistakable stamp: they are forceful and charged cinematographically, as well as reticent, stylised and musical," organisers said in a statement.
examples.source: BBC News, “Berlin honours S Korean director”

examples.text: Mr Inspector replied, with due generality and reticence, that it was always more likely that a man had done a bad thing than that he hadn't.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: She showed her usual reticence to her parents, and only said, that if Lydgate had done as she wished he would have left Middlemarch long ago.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Having or showing keen mental discernment and good judgment; wise.
etymology: From Latin sagax "of quick perception," from sagire "to perceive keenly."

examples.text: Besides, hast thou not chosen thy opportunity with wonderful little skill, indeed with no touch of that sagacity for which thou art famous?
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: A succession of adventures, so much glory, such a victorious progress! and the deep sense of his sagacity crowning every day of his inner life.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: The sagacious mind of Mr. Jefferson early saw and lamented this error, and attempts have been made, hitherto without success, to apply the amendatory power of the States to its correction.
examples.author: William Henry Harrison

definition: Optimistic or positive, especially in an apparently bad or difficult situation.
etymology: From Latin sanguineus "of blood," from sanguis "blood." In medieval humoral theory, an excess of blood made a person cheerful and confident.

examples.text: But in the face of the strengthening yen making exports less competitive and indications of weakening economic conditions ahead, observers were less sanguine.

But a Bank of Japan official took a much more sanguine view, telling Reuters that "the exchange market is apparently reacting too much, and anyone who sold the dollar on the Baker comment will regret it later on."
Meanwhile, I must say, I could not agree with my guardian on the subject of the will, and I had some sanguine hopes of Jarndyce and Jarndyce.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Grimly mocking or cynical.
etymology: From Greek sardanios, used by Homer of bitter laughter; later linked to a Sardinian plant said to contort the face of anyone who ate it.

examples.text: Old Monsieur Farival laughed sardonically at something as he looked at the sails, and Beaudelet swore at the old man under his breath.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

examples.text: He sat quietly, with a sardonic expression on his gaunt face, and spoke only when the opportunity occurred to throw in a witticism.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: The sergeant, taking note of this, gave pause to his elaborate history while he administered a sardonic comment.
examples.author: Stephen Crane

definition: Diligent, thorough, and extremely attentive to details; very concerned to avoid doing wrong.
etymology: From Latin scrupulus "a small sharp stone" — a stone in one's shoe, figuratively a small worry that pricks the conscience.

examples.text: He always wore a white neckcloth, clean indeed, but not tied with that scrupulous care which now distinguishes some of our younger clergy.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: He hoped to secure the approbation of his mistress by scrupulous obedience to all her commands, and faithful care of all that belonged to her.
examples.author: Maria Edgeworth

examples.text: The war has been waged on our part with scrupulous regard to all these obligations, and in a spirit of liberality which was never surpassed.
examples.author: James Madison

definition: Occurring at irregular intervals or only in a few places; scattered.
etymology: From Greek sporadikos "scattered," from speirein "to sow" (also in "spore").

examples.text: There was only sporadic activity for spot material, which was mainly requirement buying, they said, adding that pre-registered coffees were no longer available.
examples.source: Reuters, “Ico Quota Talks Failure Paralyse Hamburg Market”

examples.text: It would have been warm, with sporadic volcanic explosions, he says.
It has an active and smoke-misted billiard room, it is represented by baseball and football teams, and in the pool and the gymnasium a tenth of the members sporadically try to reduce.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: Enduring pain or hardship without showing feelings or complaining.
etymology: From Greek Stōikos, from Stoa Poikilē, the "Painted Porch" in Athens where Zeno of Citium taught his philosophy around 300 BC.

examples.text: The suppression of grief was also helped by a decline in religious ritual and by a period of major wars in which soldiers, and by implication all of us, were expected to bear death with stoicism, says Jalland.
Every truck that made its way from the factories to the freight-stations was guarded by a policeman, trying to look stoical beside the scab driver.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: Is not modern stoicism, built though it be on Christianity, as great an outrage on human nature as was the stoicism of the ancients?
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: A person who acts obsequiously toward someone important to gain advantage.
etymology: From Greek sykophantēs "informer, slanderer," literally "fig-revealer." The origin of the image is unclear.

examples.text: Was it her fault if she did not possess those sycophantic arts which her hypocritical nephew, Pitt Crawley, practised?
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: Ahab did not like Micaiah, because he never prophesied good concerning him, but evil; probably he liked the sycophant son of Chenaannah better; yet might Ahab have escaped a bloody death, had he but stopped his ears to flattery, and opened them to faithful counsel.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: With other black boys the strife was not so fiercely sunny: their youth shrunk into tasteless sycophancy, or into silent hatred of the pale world about them and mocking distrust of everything white; or wasted itself in a bitter cry, Why did God make me an outcast and a stranger in mine own house?
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

definition: Reserved or uncommunicative in speech; saying little.
etymology: From Latin taciturnus, from tacitus "silent," from tacere "to be silent."

examples.text: The next day, which was Sunday, passed nearly in the same manner as regarded their taciturnity, Bathsheba going to church both morning and afternoon.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: At Gravier's where they ate, and in the evening at the Versailles or at the Closerie des Lilas Clutton was inclined to taciturnity.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: There she sat, staid and taciturn-looking, as usual, in her brown stuff gown, her check apron, white handkerchief, and cap.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

definition: Excessive confidence or boldness; audacity.
etymology: From Latin temeritas "rashness," from temere "blindly, by chance."

examples.text: An Elizabeth in brain and a Mary Stuart in spirit, she often performed actions of the greatest temerity with a manner of extreme discretion.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: He stared up disapprovingly over his eye-glasses as Mr. Pontellier entered, wondering who had the temerity to disturb him at that hour of the morning.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

examples.text: 'I looked up again at the crouching white shape, and the full temerity of my voyage came suddenly upon me.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

definition: Tending to keep a firm hold of something; persistent and determined.
etymology: From Latin tenax "holding fast," from tenere "to hold."

examples.text: The researchers did, however, confirm just how tenacious the bacteria are.
Still, when Hans, rather late in the day, got able to use his own eyes, Deronda had tenacity enough to try hard and recover his lost ground.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: All this was incomprehensible, and then, with the tenacity peculiar to prophets of bad news, the failure was put off until the end of September.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: A state of physical or mental inactivity; lethargy.
etymology: From Latin torpor "numbness," from torpere "to be numb." The electric torpedo fish was named for numbing its prey.

examples.text: I lie awake while thou sleepest, I weep while thou singest, I am faint with fasting while thou art sluggish and torpid from pure repletion.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: The bold and reckless young blood of ten-years back was subjugated and was turned into a torpid, submissive, middle-aged, stout gentleman.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: When there she threw herself on the bed with her clothes on, and lay in apparent torpor, as she had done once before on a memorable day of grief.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Overused and consequently of little import; lacking originality or freshness.
etymology: From Latin tritus "worn," past participle of terere "to rub." An expression worn smooth by use.

examples.text: Then there was a little more trite conversation between Mr. Arabin and Mr. Harding—trite, and hard, and vapid, and senseless.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: For it is an observation, as true as it is trite, that there is nothing men differ so readily about as the payment of money.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: With the majority such an opinion is shelved with all those trite aphorisms which require some catastrophe to bring their tremendous meanings thoroughly home.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: Eager or quick to argue or fight; aggressively defiant.
etymology: From Latin truculentus "fierce, savage," from trux "fierce."

examples.text: She really was a most charming girl, and might have passed for a captive fairy, whom that truculent Ogre, Old Barley, had pressed into his service.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: On state occasions he would tread on his master's heels, one hand on the haft of his kriss, keeping the common people at a distance by his truculent brooding glances.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: There is, in world affairs, a steady course to be followed between an assertion of strength that is truculent and a confession of helplessness that is cowardly.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Present, appearing, or found everywhere.
etymology: From Latin ubique "everywhere," from ubi "where."

examples.text: Cheap radio chips that are replacing the ubiquitous barcode are a threat to privacy and susceptible to computer viruses, scientists say.
The first version of the service is part of Google's expanding efforts to be a ubiquitous search engine for people to find what they want on the web and beyond.
examples.source: BBC News, “Google launches TV search service”

examples.text: Sallie Gardiner was absorbed in keeping her white pique dress clean and chattering with the ubiquitous Fred, who kept Beth in constant terror by his pranks.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

definition: To alternate or waver between different opinions or actions; to be indecisive.
etymology: From Latin vacillare "to sway, totter."

examples.text: He honestly mistook his sensuality for romantic emotion, his vacillation for the artistic temperament, and his idleness for philosophic calm.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: However much of vacillating whim there might have been in his entrance on matrimony, there was no vacillating in his interpretation of the bond.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: We must avoid extremes, for vacillation between extremes is inefficient, costly, and destructive of morale.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Offering nothing that is stimulating or challenging; bland and lifeless.
etymology: From Latin vapidus "flat, flavorless," used of wine that had lost its life; related to vapor.

examples.text: Such stale vapid rejected cabbage-leaf and cabbage-stalk dress, such damaged-orange countenance, such squashed pulp of humanity, are open to the day nowhere else.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: "Sacrifice the world for love!" she said in answer to some renewed vapid declaration of his passion.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: Much did she censure the attenuated Cupids who encircle the ceiling of the Queen's Hall, inclining each to each with vapid gesture, and clad in sallow pantaloons, on which the October sunlight struck.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: Showing or motivated by susceptibility to bribery; corrupt. (Not "venial," which means pardonable.)
etymology: From Latin venalis "for sale," from venum "sale."

examples.text: This peculiar felicity of situation has, in a great degree, contributed to preserve the liberty which that country to this day enjoys, in spite of the prevalent venality and corruption.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: There was another attraction in his profession: it wanted reform, and gave a man an opportunity for some indignant resolve to reject its venal decorations and other humbug, and to be the possessor of genuine though undemanded qualifications.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: If that solitary suffrage can be obtained by foreign nations by flattery or menaces, by fraud or violence, by terror, intrigue, or venality, the Government may not be the choice of the American people, but of foreign nations.
examples.author: John Adams

definition: To regard with great respect; to revere.
etymology: From Latin venerari "to adore, revere," related to Venus.

examples.text: It was not the most promising party to travel with and hope to gain a higher veneration for religion through the example of its devotees.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: For forty or fifty years past, from the times of former elders, no visitors had entered that cell without feelings of the profoundest veneration.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: It degrades to the purposes of wily craft the plan of rule our fathers established and bequeathed to us as an object of our love and veneration.
examples.author: Grover Cleveland

definition: Conformity to facts; accuracy; habitual truthfulness.
etymology: From Medieval Latin veracitas, from Latin verax "truthful," from verus "true."

examples.text: "We still want to believe the veracity of the stem cell lines, which we hope will be verified by a world-renowned lab, not some incompetent committee from Seoul National University," Hwang said.
Benedetto maintained the truth of what he had said, and accompanied it with details that did more honor to his imagination than to his veracity.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: Nature, he knows, has a language of her own, which she uses with strict veracity, and he considers himself an adept in the language.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Using or expressed in more words than are needed.
etymology: From Latin verbosus, from verbum "word."

examples.text: The persecutors denied that there was any particular gift in Mr. Chadband's piling verbose flights of stairs, one upon another, after this fashion.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: There was evidently not space enough for his drunken verbosity and Mitya not only filled the margins but had written the last line right across the rest.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: What he had to say was confused, halting, and verbose; but Philip knew the words which served as the text of his rambling discourse.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: To clear someone of blame or suspicion; to show to be right or justified.
etymology: From Latin vindicare "to lay claim to, avenge, set free," from vindex "claimant, avenger."

examples.text: The Federal Government says it has been vindicated by the ruling.

In a statement, Mr Rangel said the land reform is not against the constitution, which permits private property, while stressing the efforts are to "vindicate social and economically" years of inequality in the country.
Once again, Lily had withdrawn from an ambiguous situation in time to save her self-respect, but too late for public vindication.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: Liable to change rapidly and unpredictably, especially for the worse; (of a substance) easily evaporated.
etymology: From Latin volatilis "flying," from volare "to fly." First used of birds, then of substances that "fly off" as vapor.

examples.text: The measure, confirmed by a brokerage firm here, has effectively cut off all foreign participation in Venezuela's volatile currency market.
Over the longer term, stock market funds have outperformed other types of investment, although in the shorter term they can be volatile.
examples.source: BBC News, “Giving financial gifts to children”

examples.text: It was also distilled to a volatile salts for fainting ladies, the same way that the horns of the male deer are manufactured into hartshorn.
examples.author: Herman Melville

definition: Speaking or spoken incessantly and fluently.
etymology: From Latin volubilis "rolling, turning," from volvere "to roll." Words that roll off the tongue.

examples.text: When he presented himself again he was racked with a headache—penitent, and volubly afraid that in his drunkenness he might have been indiscreet.
examples.author: Rudyard Kipling

examples.text: The poor girl spoke these words with a spirit and volubility which Rebecca had never before seen in her, and before which the latter was quite dumb.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: So situated, she was powerless to check Jo, who seemed possessed by a spirit of mischief, and talked away as volubly as the lady.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

definition: Having or showing great energy or enthusiasm in pursuit of a cause or objective.
etymology: From Greek zēlos "ardor, jealousy." "Jealous" comes from the same word by way of French.

examples.text: His friend, Saxon Spence, leader of Devon county Labour group, lays the blame for any lack of campaigning zeal on one issue above all others.
examples.source: BBC News, “Labour's core support takes stock”

examples.text: The head of the Ranger uranium mine in the Northern Territory says new entrants to the uranium industry should prepare themselves for zealous government regulation.
This icon of the Venerable Sergius, the servant of God and zealous champion of old of our country's weal, is offered to Your Imperial Majesty.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)
